findings.text: The first lede tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is and what makes it different. Someone who reads only this paragraph can say what the project is.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it shows Athena's work on a real project. That is the only answer to 'why it matters'. Nothing on the page tells the reader what Athena does for them on their own repository.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The page gives a next step right at the top and links it to a Next steps section with a repo link and two commands. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install step lists no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or AI model credentials. It also doesn't say what 'athena ask "add a changelog"' will do or where. A newcomer could get stuck here or be surprised by the result.
findings.source: Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh

findings.text: The page is at Athena's address, but its title and almost all of its content describe another project (firstmate). A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to wade through firstmate's internals to find two sentences about Athena.
findings.source: Athena explains how firstmate handles work

findings.text: Sections like the transition cards (t1–t11), Counters and 'Why it is built this way' are dense: exit codes, pending-close records, places-held. They help a firstmate maintainer, but a newcomer to Athena gets little from them except a sense of how detailed the output is.
The 'Start here' section, its 'Words used first' list and the full Glossary define nearly every term before it is used. The firstmate study is easy to follow for anyone who wants to read it.
The page says honestly that nothing was run ('every claim is marked read') and that a first reading missed several paths. This builds trust in the claims being shown.

The 'concurrency entry' does not cite secondmate claim c44. I searched the page and c44 appears only in the secondmate glossary entry and in the claim list. This sentence in finding f2 therefore points to something the page does not show.
findings.source: The page attaches those claims to the counter, to the relaunch transition, to the queued state and to the concurrency entry.
